claims.text: Resistance to simultaneous wear and corrosion in HEAs is governed by their ability to form a multi-component, self-healing passivating oxide film.
Sluggish diffusion stabilizes the self-healing passivating oxide film in HEAs.
Chemical complexity, particularly at grain boundaries, stabilizes the passivating oxide film.
The proposed HEA has equiatomic or near-equiatomic ratios of multiple principal elements.
The proposed initial microstructure contains fine grains and chemically segregated grain-boundary regions.
The controlled comparison will include combined wear-corrosion, corrosion-only, and wear-only conditions.
Formation and maintenance of a multi-component passivating film occur both at the surface and along grain boundaries.
The sluggish diffusion behavior inherent to HEAs enhances formation and maintenance of the passivating film.
Localized damage under combined mechanical and corrosive stress is rapidly mitigated by self-healing of the oxide layer.
Multiple alloying elements contribute different oxidation kinetics that enable the oxide layer to reform continuously after wear-induced disruption.
Continuous oxide reformation maintains a barrier against further chemical attack.
The HEA will have a lower combined wear-corrosion degradation rate than a mechanically matched, chemically simpler conventional alloy.
Stable, regenerating passivation mitigates both the wear and corrosion components of degradation.
The combined test will exhibit a nonlinear improvement in resistance even though standalone wear and corrosion each cause moderate degradation.
The hypothesis applies when oxide reformation kinetics can keep pace with mechanically induced film damage.
The proposed protection may fail under very low pH, high chloride concentration, and high mechanical stress because oxide formation cannot keep pace with damage.
Failure to observe either a significantly lower combined degradation rate or oxide-film reformation in the HEA would falsify the proposed governing mechanism.
